title_en: My Gym Membership and Other Fictions
title_ru: Мой абонемент в спортзал и другие вымыслы
description_ru: Самоироничная история человека, который каждый январь платит за спортзал и находит всё более изобретательные причины туда не ходить.
text:
Every January, with the solemnity of a man signing a treaty, I join a gym. I fill in the form, I smile at the young person behind the desk, who is invariably built like a kitchen appliance, and I hand over my bank details with the serene conviction that this time it will be different. I have done this for eleven consecutive years. In that time, I estimate that I have attended on forty-three occasions, which, when divided into the sum I have paid, means that each visit has cost me about the same as a modest second-hand car.

The first week is always glorious. I arrive on Monday in new trainers, as white and unmarked as a freshly painted wall, and I walk through the glass doors with the swagger of a man who has been training for years. I lift things. I place my towel carefully on the machine like a person staking a claim on foreign territory. For forty-five minutes I run on a treadmill, watching television with the sound off, and I leave with a feeling of virtue so intense that I buy a large cake on the way home, as a reward.

By Wednesday, a certain stiffness has set in. By Thursday, I am unable to descend a staircase without gripping the banister like a man on the deck of a ship in a storm. My legs have developed independent opinions, none of them friendly, and I find myself walking in the stiff and careful manner of a robot that has been asked to carry something heavy. A colleague asked on Friday whether I had hurt myself. "Training," I said, with a bravery I could not feel, and went to sit down, very slowly, in a chair.

By the second week, my commitment has become flexible. I do not decide to skip the gym. Skipping implies a choice, and choices are for people without excuses. Instead I discover obstacles. On Tuesday, it was raining, and the gym is a ten-minute walk from my flat. On Wednesday it was dark, which I considered a safety issue. On Thursday I felt a mysterious twinge in my left knee that disappeared when I went to the pub, and on Friday I decided to rest in order to prevent a twinge in my right one. Anyone who calls this laziness has failed to understand the sophistication of the system.

Over the years, I have developed a repertoire of excuses so elaborate that it ought to be taught in universities. I have had imaginary deadlines, imaginary colds and an imaginary aunt who needed me urgently, although I do not have an aunt. I have claimed that my trainers were at the cobbler's, that the gym smelled of disinfectant and that my horoscope had advised against exercise on a Wednesday. Once, in a spasm of creativity, I claimed that I could not go because I was reading a book about fitness, which, as it happens, I had not opened.

It is worth describing the people who do attend. There is a tall man with the physique of a Greek statue who spends his evenings admiring himself, from various angles, in a large mirror. There is an elderly lady who swims a hundred lengths of the pool every morning and who regards me, whenever I lurch into the changing room, with the cold pity of a lighthouse watching a rowing boat. And there is a small, cheerful instructor named Brett, who is incapable of discouragement. "Come on, you've got this!" he says, to people who plainly have not got this, and who may never get this, and who would like to be left alone.

My friend Marguerite, who runs marathons for pleasure, which tells you all you need to know about her, suggested that I should find an "exercise buddy" and hold myself accountable. I recruited my neighbour, a gentle accountant named Ferdinand, who agreed on the condition that we should meet at the gym at six in the morning. We managed it twice. On the first occasion, we stared at each other with the haunted eyes of men at a railway station at dawn, and on the second, we agreed that we had probably achieved enough for one lifetime and went for breakfast. Ferdinand has since moved to Portugal. I like to think that it was nothing to do with me.

You may wonder why I do not simply cancel the membership. The answer is that I cannot bear to admit defeat. Cancelling would be an acknowledgement that the person I imagined myself becoming, lean, disciplined and cheerful about early mornings, is not coming, and I would rather lose money than lose him. The direct debit, in this sense, is a form of hope. For the price of a monthly sum, I buy the right to believe in a better version of myself, and I think many people do the same. Gyms, I suspect, know this perfectly well; their entire business model depends on our optimism, and our absence.

This year, however, I decided to try something different. On the second of January, I went to the gym, and instead of running on the treadmill, which I find as stimulating as a dentist's waiting room, I took a class. The class was called "Gentle Stretch", and I imagined an hour of pleasant relaxation. It was instead a prolonged and public display of my own inflexibility, conducted in front of a mirror, in which I could not touch my toes, my knees or, at one stage, any part of my body below the chest. The instructor told us to "breathe into the stretch", and I breathed into it with such sincerity that I made a small sound, like a kettle, and the lady beside me opened her eyes.

I shall be back on Monday, however. I have put the date in my diary, and laid out my trainers, and told several people. If you see me, please ask how it is going. And if I tell you that I have been to the gym every day, kindly look at my face for the telltale signs of an invented aunt.

questions.question: How many times has the writer attended the gym in eleven years?
What are some of the excuses the writer invents?
questions.answer: Imaginary deadlines, colds and an aunt.

questions.question: Why does the writer not cancel the membership?
questions.answer: He cannot admit defeat; it is a form of hope.

questions.question: What went wrong in the Gentle Stretch class?
questions.answer: He could not touch his toes and made a kettle-like noise.
